segments.text: Mariko
My university classmate
Became the first woman to serve as factory manager
At a major manufacturer
It was when she was forty
She had graduated from the engineering department
And at first worked as a technician
The workers on the floor were all men
And at first she was not accepted
As a peer
Mary Cole learned everything
From the safety procedures
On the shop floor
To the operating methods
Of each machine
She wore the same clothing
As the workers
And walked the factory
From morning till night
After ten years
She climbed the steps of promotion
Becoming section chief, department head
And then factory manager
This was unusual in the industry
Despite Mary Co's appointment as factory manager
There were voices of both support and objection
Can a woman with a home and children to raise
Carry such a responsible post?
Some asked, but the results were clear
Under her management, the factory's productivity rose and accidents decreased
From a woman's viewpoint, she also promoted a workplace where people could work more easily
The glass ceiling, the invisible wall that blocks women's promotion
Still exists today
But as pioneers like Mariko increase
The wall that's being broken little by little
Gender equality is not only a women's issue
It is also an economic necessity
For maximizing the output of society as a whole
A society cannot develop without making use of the talent of half its population
Mariko has both the strength not to yield
When confronted with obstacles and kindness toward others
She has become a role model
For the next generation of women leaders
